newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary's austerity cuts GDP growth rate - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Hungary's austerity cuts GDP growth rate - analysts.

text.p: Hungary's preliminary 1.5 percent GDP growth figure for 1995 is as expected and shows the country's austerity programme had slowed down the economy, analysts said.
The Central Statistical Office data published on Friday showed GDP growth dropping from 2.9 percent in 1994, matching previous estimates.
They said the austerity programme, launched by former Finance Minister Lajos Bokros in March 1995 to rein in the soaring budget and current account deficits, was the cause of the drop in GDP growth.
"The Bokros package caused the fall in domestic demand, investments halted and industrial output decreased," said Laszlo Batora of Raiffeisen Securities.

The austerity programme, which included devaluations, imposition of an eight percent surcharge on imports, and social spending cuts, restored the balance of the budget and the current account, but led to a slump in real wages and had a cooling effect on the economy, analysts said.
"Economic restrictions were perhaps oversized," GKI Economic Research Institute's Judit Barta added.
She said the government measures made imports expensive and this hurt many firms which need imports for their production.
Analysts said the GDP growth fell further this year, but was likely to rise in the fourth quarter, leaving full 1996 growth below one percent.
The think-tank Kopint-Datorg Rt said in a recent report that investments are likely to grow by only three percent this year as companies were discouraged by low domestic demand.
But if real wages keep their real value in 1997, investments could increase by five to six percent, in which case GDP would grow by two percent, Kopint-Datorg added.
The government forecasts static real wages and an unchanged current account deficit along with two to three percent GDP growth for 1997, and stronger GDP growth in subsequent years.
The government has said it will abolish the import surcharge, which has already been cut by two percent, in the second half of next year.
Analysts said the two percent GDP growth target for 1997 was realistic.
They said Hungary's growth rate was low compared with other central and east European countries, but the figures were not comparable because statistics systems differed.

Andras Inotai, head of the government's task group of experts for European integration, said Hungary's statistics do not include important items such as data on the informal economy. Including these, the final growth figure may be double the official forecast, he said.
